entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: While someone is still a young child, often earlier than is usual for the activity mentioned.
entries.usage: Common in biographies, interviews, news and conversation, often with *start*, *learn*, *show* (a talent) or *lose* (a parent). *From an early age* stresses that something began in childhood and continued. *At a young age* means the same and is just as common.
entries.pattern: start / learn / show talent + at an early age; from an early age
examples: Most players on the national hockey team started skating **at an early age**, some as young as three.
She lost her father **at an early age** and was raised by her grandparents.
Doctors recommend checking children's eyesight **at an early age**, since some problems are easier to treat then.

drill.sentence: My grandmother taught me to cook {{at an early age}}; I was making pancakes by myself when I was six.
drill.hint: when I was still a small child (preposition *at*; adjective not *young*)

entries.related: *at a young age* — the same; *from an early age* — since childhood and continuing; *early on* — at the beginning of a process, not about childhood.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Something that is very effective for achieving a goal or causing change; it is often a method, idea or technology rather than a physical tool.
entries.usage: Common in talks, journalism, education and marketing, usually as *a powerful tool for* + noun or *-ing*, or *a powerful tool to* + verb. Typical subjects are abstract: *humor, data, education, a simple question*. In ads and corporate speech it can sound like a cliché, so in careful writing say what the tool actually does.
entries.pattern: a powerful tool for + noun / -ing; a powerful tool to + verb
examples: A simple shopping list is **a powerful tool** for staying on budget at the grocery store.
In a tense meeting, a little humor can be **a powerful tool** for calming everyone down.
Satellite images have become **a powerful tool** for tracking wildfires as they spread.

drill.sentence: Teachers say that reading aloud to kids every night is {{a powerful tool}} for building their vocabulary.
drill.hint: a very effective means (adjective: not *great*, *useful* or *effective*)

entries.related: *an effective tool* — plainer, less emphatic; *a game changer* — informal, something that changes a situation completely; *a double-edged sword* — useful but also risky.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Having no connection at all with something else.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, emails and explanations, either to say that two things have no link or to change the topic: *On a completely unrelated note, …* The usual pattern is *completely unrelated to* + noun. *Totally unrelated* is more casual, and *entirely unrelated* a little more formal.
entries.pattern: be completely unrelated (to + noun); on a completely unrelated note
examples: The two fires broke out on the same night, but police say they were **completely unrelated**.
On a **completely unrelated** note, does anyone know a good dentist around here?
The app kept crashing, but the problem was **completely unrelated** to the update we'd installed that morning.

drill.sentence: I blamed my headaches on my new glasses, but the eye doctor said the two things were {{completely unrelated}}.
drill.hint: not connected in any way (adverb: not *totally* or *entirely*)

entries.related: *irrelevant* — not important for the question being discussed; *unconnected* — the same idea, a bit more formal; *closely related* — the opposite.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A person or thing that is very useful to a group or organization and helps it succeed.
entries.usage: Very common in job interviews, cover letters, references and sports or business news. The usual pattern is *a valuable asset to* + group (*for* is also used). About a person it is strong, professional praise; among friends it can sound like HR language, so it is often used half jokingly.
entries.pattern: be / prove (to be) a valuable asset to + team / company / community
examples: Her fluent Spanish made her **a valuable asset** to the clinic, where many patients spoke little English.
A friend with a pickup truck is **a valuable asset** when you're moving.
The team signed the young shortstop to a three-year deal, calling him **a valuable asset**.

drill.sentence: With twenty years in the hotel business, Marco would be {{a valuable asset}} to our new restaurant.
drill.hint: someone extremely useful to have (adjective: not *great*, *real* or *huge*)

entries.related: *an asset to* — the same without the adjective; *a liability* — the opposite, someone who causes problems; *a team player* — someone who works well with others.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To carry out a scientific or practical test in order to find something out or check an idea.
entries.usage: *Run* is the usual verb in conversation and in labs; *conduct* or *carry out* an experiment sounds more formal, and *do an experiment* is typical at school. It is also used for informal trials of a new habit, rule or idea, often with *to see if* or *to see whether*.
entries.pattern: run an experiment (on + subject) (to see if / whether …)
examples: To find out which fertilizer works best, we **ran an experiment** with three rows of tomatoes.
Our school **ran an experiment** this year: no homework on weekends, and grades actually went up.
The team **ran the experiment** twice to make sure the result wasn't a fluke.

drill.sentence: I'm {{running an experiment}} this month: no coffee after lunch, to see if I sleep better.
drill.hint: carrying out a test on myself (verb: not *doing* or *trying*)

entries.related: *conduct an experiment* — more formal; *carry out an experiment* — formal, common in reports; *trial and error* — trying things until one works.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Whatever happens, no matter how much effort, money or risk it takes.
entries.usage: Shows strong determination and usually comes at the end of the clause. *Avoid something at all costs* is the most common pattern and often works as a warning or advice. *Win at all costs* is often critical, suggesting that someone ignores fairness or rules.
entries.pattern: avoid / protect / win + something + at all costs
examples: The guide told us to stay on the trail **at all costs**, because the snow on the ridge was unstable.
Some youth coaches teach kids to win **at all costs**, and that takes the fun out of the game.
The airline wanted to avoid a strike **at all costs**, so it raised its offer twice.

drill.sentence: If you visit the city in August, avoid driving downtown {{at all costs}}; the traffic is unbelievable.
drill.hint: regardless of the price or effort (preposition + *all* + noun; not *no matter what*)

entries.related: *no matter what* — the same idea, more conversational; *whatever it takes* — stresses willingness to do anything; *at any cost* — very similar, slightly less common.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To check, usually through an experiment or by collecting data, whether a proposed explanation is true.
entries.usage: Mainly scientific and academic, often followed by a *that*-clause: *test the hypothesis that …*. Results *support* or *contradict* a hypothesis rather than *prove* it, and the plural is *hypotheses*. In everyday talk it is used half jokingly for informal checks: *Let's test that hypothesis.*
entries.pattern: test the hypothesis that …; test a hypothesis about + topic
examples: Scientists **tested the hypothesis** by giving half the mice a high-sugar diet and comparing their weight.
My brother thinks our cat meows at night because she's bored, so he's **testing that hypothesis** with a laser toy.
To **test the hypothesis** that her headaches came from caffeine, her doctor asked her to stop drinking coffee for two weeks.

drill.sentence: The coach suspected the 6 a.m. practices were making his players tired, so he moved practice to the afternoon to {{test that hypothesis}}.
drill.hint: check whether that explanation was right (noun: not *theory*)

entries.related: *test a theory* — very close and more common in everyday speech; *confirm a hypothesis* — show it is supported; *a hunch* — an informal guess, not yet tested.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Knowing a lot about current facts and events, or about a particular subject, because you read, listen and ask.
entries.usage: Used as praise for people (*a well-informed reader*) and for choices based on good information (*a well-informed decision*). Before a noun it is hyphenated; after a verb, both *well informed* and *well-informed* are common, depending on the style guide. Typical patterns are *be / stay / keep well informed about* or *on* a topic.
entries.pattern: be / stay well informed (about / on + topic); a well-informed + person / decision
examples: My grandfather reads three newspapers a day, so he's always **well informed** about what's happening in town.
Before you agree to surgery, make sure you're **well informed** about the risks.
The tour guide was surprisingly **well informed** and answered every question about the cathedral's history.

drill.sentence: She follows the news closely and talks to people on all sides, so she's usually {{well informed}} about local issues.
drill.hint: knowing a lot about the facts (adverb + participle; not *up to date*)

entries.related: *knowledgeable* — knowing a lot about a subject, less about current events; *up to date* — having the latest information; *misinformed* — the opposite, believing false information.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To ask a large number of people the same questions in order to collect information about their opinions or behavior.
entries.usage: A little formal and common in reports, news and business writing; in conversation people more often say *do*, *run* or *send out a survey*. The group follows *of* or *among*, and the topic follows *on* or *about*: *a survey of local businesses*. *Survey* is also a verb: *We surveyed 500 parents.*
entries.pattern: conduct a survey (of / among + group) (on / about + topic)
examples: The city **conducted a survey** of 2,000 residents to find out how they get to work.
Our building's management **conducted a survey** to see whether tenants wanted a gym or a bike room.
The researchers **conducted a survey** of nurses at twelve hospitals about burnout and overtime.

drill.sentence: Before planning the school festival, the parents' association {{conducted a survey}} to find out which activities families wanted most.
drill.hint: formally asked many people the same questions (formal verb; not *did*, *ran* or *carried out*)

mistake.wrong: We made a survey among our customers.
mistake.right: We conducted a survey among our customers.
mistake.why: *Make a survey* comes from German *eine Umfrage machen*; English says *conduct*, *carry out*, *do* or *run* a survey.

entries.related: *carry out a survey* — also formal; *take a poll* — ask people's opinion, often quickly or about one question; *a questionnaire* — the list of questions itself.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A job for people with little or no experience, usually at the lowest level of a company or field.
entries.usage: Very common in job ads, career advice and conversation: *apply for / land / start in an entry-level position*. *Entry-level job* and *entry-level role* are just as common; *position* sounds a bit more formal. *Entry-level* also describes cheap, basic products: *an entry-level laptop*.
entries.pattern: apply for / land / start in + an entry-level position (at + company)
examples: Right out of college, she took **an entry-level position** at a bank, answering phones and filing paperwork.
Many **entry-level positions** now ask for two years of experience, which frustrates new graduates.
My cousin started in **an entry-level position** at the hotel and became general manager ten years later.

drill.sentence: After his internship, he applied for {{an entry-level position}} at an advertising agency, hoping to work his way up.
drill.hint: a starting job for beginners (noun: not *job* or *role*)

entries.related: *a junior position* — low in rank, but may need some experience; *an internship* — temporary training, often unpaid or low-paid; *a senior position* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To go to a lecture and be present while it is given.
entries.usage: *Attend* is neutral to formal and common in announcements, emails and reports; in conversation students usually say *go to a lecture* or *go to class*. *Attend* takes a direct object with no preposition. The speaker *gives* or *delivers* the lecture.
entries.pattern: attend a lecture (on + topic / by + speaker)
examples: More than three hundred people **attended the lecture** on the history of jazz at the public library.
Since he retired, my dad **attends a free lecture** at the community college every Thursday.
Students who **attend lectures** regularly tend to get better grades than those who only read the slides.

drill.sentence: During our trip to Boston, we {{attended a lecture}} at the science museum about black holes.
drill.hint: were in the audience for a talk (formal verb; not *went to*)

mistake.wrong: Over two hundred people attended to the lecture.
mistake.right: Over two hundred people attended the lecture.
mistake.why: *Attend* an event takes no preposition; *attend to* means *deal with* or *take care of*, as in *attend to a patient*.

entries.related: *sit in on a lecture* — attend without being enrolled; *give a lecture* — what the speaker does; *skip a lecture* — informal, not go.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Homes that people with low or modest incomes can pay for; in the US it often means units whose rent or price is limited by law or subsidies.
entries.usage: Very common in news, city planning and local debates: *build / create / a shortage of / a lack of affordable housing*. In American news it often refers to a specific category of income-restricted units, not just any cheap home. *Housing* is uncountable, so count with *units*, *homes* or *apartments*.
entries.pattern: build / create / a shortage of + affordable housing
examples: Many nurses and teachers can't find **affordable housing** near the hospitals and schools where they work.
The city plans to turn the old factory into three hundred units of **affordable housing**.
We moved two hours away because there was no **affordable housing** anywhere near my job.

drill.sentence: Rents have doubled in ten years, so the waiting list for {{affordable housing}} in our town now has over two thousand names.
drill.hint: homes that people on modest incomes can pay for (adjective: not *public* or *low-income*)

mistake.wrong: The city is building many affordable housings downtown.
mistake.right: The city is building a lot of affordable housing downtown.
mistake.why: *Housing* is uncountable; to count, say *affordable homes*, *apartments* or *units*.

entries.related: *public housing* — owned and run by the government; *low-income housing* — the same idea, more direct; *market-rate housing* — rented or sold at normal prices.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: In order to help, protect, keep or achieve something or someone.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and writing: *for the sake of the kids*, *for the sake of time / clarity / peace*. With a person, the possessive form is usual: *for my sake*, *for your mother's sake*. *For the sake of it* means *for no real reason*, as in *arguing for the sake of it*.
entries.pattern: for the sake of + noun (argument / time / clarity); for someone's sake
examples: They stayed together **for the sake of** the children, but everyone could see they were unhappy.
**For the sake of** simplicity, let's split the bill evenly instead of figuring out who ordered what.
He finally quit smoking **for the sake of** his health after a scare at the doctor's office.

drill.sentence: Let's assume, {{for the sake of}} argument, that the house sells for the asking price. Can we afford the new one?
drill.hint: as a purely imagined case — four words, ending in *of* (not the possessive form)

entries.related: *for the benefit of* — to help or be useful to someone; *on behalf of* — representing someone; *for its own sake* — because it is good in itself.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To decide to remember something for later, without writing it down.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and storytelling, usually followed by *to* + verb or a *that*-clause. It often hints that the person may still forget. *Make* is the usual verb (*take a mental note* is also heard), and *make a note of* without *mental* means writing it down.
entries.pattern: make a mental note to + verb / (that) …
examples: I passed a new bakery on my way to work and **made a mental note** to stop by on Saturday.
She **made a mental note** that her new boss hated long emails.
I noticed the tires looked low and **made a mental note** to check the pressure, and then I completely forgot.

drill.sentence: A guy at the gym said his knee surgery went really well, so I {{made a mental note}} to ask him for his surgeon's name.
drill.hint: decided to remember, without writing it down (verb + adjective + noun)

entries.related: *make a note of* — write something down; *keep in mind* — remember and consider later; *jot down* — write quickly.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: Seriously harmed or broken, often so much that repair is difficult or impossible.
entries.usage: Very common in news after storms, fires and accidents, and in everyday talk about cars, homes and phones. It also works for abstract things such as trust, a reputation or a relationship. *Severely damaged* and *heavily damaged* are close variants that sound more like news reports.
entries.pattern: be / get badly damaged (in + fire / storm / crash; by + smoke / water)
examples: Our roof was **badly damaged** in the storm, and water was dripping into the kitchen.
The painting was **badly damaged** by smoke, but the museum's restorers managed to save it.
Years of broken promises had **badly damaged** their trust in each other.

drill.sentence: The car was so {{badly damaged}} in the crash that the insurance company declared it a total loss.
drill.hint: seriously harmed (adverb: not *severely* or *heavily*)

entries.related: *slightly damaged* — the opposite degree; *beyond repair* — too damaged to fix; *totaled* — American informal, a car too damaged to be worth repairing.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A period when business activity, jobs and spending fall and the economy gets weaker.
entries.usage: Common in news, business writing and conversation about jobs and prices. It sounds less dramatic than *recession* or *crisis*, and it does not have a technical definition. Typical patterns are *during / in an economic downturn* and *be hit by an economic downturn*.
entries.pattern: during / survive / be hit by + an economic downturn
examples: During **the economic downturn**, the restaurant cut its hours and laid off half its staff.
Luxury brands usually suffer first in **an economic downturn**, while discount stores often do well.
Our emergency savings helped us get through **the economic downturn** without selling the house.

drill.sentence: Many families put off buying new cars during {{the economic downturn}}, so dealers offered big discounts.
drill.hint: the period of weak business and falling jobs (adjective + noun; not *recession*, *slump* or *crisis*)

mistake.wrong: Many small shops closed during the economical downturn.
mistake.right: Many small shops closed during the economic downturn.
mistake.why: *Economic* means *related to the economy*; *economical* means *saving money*, as in *an economical car*.

entries.related: *a recession* — a serious downturn, with a technical meaning in economics; *a slump* — informal, a sudden fall; *an upturn* — the opposite, a period of growth.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To earn a very large amount of money, usually from business, investments or a successful product.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, biographies and news. Use *in* for the field, *from* or *on* for the source, and *-ing* for the activity: *make a fortune in real estate / on the stock market / selling phone cases*. In casual speech it is often an exaggeration or a joke about a good idea.
entries.pattern: make a fortune in + field / from + source / -ing
examples: His great-grandfather **made a fortune** in the oil business and bought half the land in the county.
If you could invent a phone battery that lasts a week, you'd **make a fortune**.
These cookies are amazing; you could **make a fortune** selling them at the farmers market.

drill.sentence: She bought a few apartments in Brooklyn in the 1990s, sold them last year and {{made a fortune}}.
drill.hint: earned a huge amount of money (not the idiom with *killing*)

entries.related: *make a killing* — informal, earn a lot quickly, often from one deal; *cost a fortune* — be very expensive; *a small fortune* — ironic, a lot of money.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A large amount of money lost by a business or investor, or a large number of people, animals or things lost in a war or disaster.
entries.usage: Common in business news and war reporting, with the verbs *suffer*, *report*, *take* and *inflict*. In business it means money; in war it means soldiers killed or wounded and equipment destroyed. *Heavy* is the standard adjective here; *big* and *huge losses* are more casual.
entries.pattern: suffer / report / take + heavy losses (on + investment)
examples: The airline reported **heavy losses** after a year of canceled flights and half-empty planes.
Both armies suffered **heavy losses** in the battle, which lasted almost a week.
My uncle took **heavy losses** on his stocks when the market crashed, so he's delaying retirement.

drill.sentence: The drought hit the region hard, and many cattle ranchers suffered {{heavy losses}}.
drill.hint: a large amount of money and livestock gone (adjective: not *big*, *huge* or *major*)

entries.related: *take a hit* — informal, lose money or suffer damage; *break even* — neither win nor lose money; *casualties* — people killed or injured in a war or accident.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To earn enough money to cover your regular living costs, such as rent, food and utilities.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, often about a job that is not exciting or not your real passion: *Acting is my dream, but bartending pays the bills.* The subject can be a person or the job or income itself. It also keeps its literal meaning of paying the bills that arrive each month.
entries.pattern: something pays the bills; struggle / help to pay the bills
examples: Writing poetry doesn't **pay the bills**, so she works as a paralegal during the day.
After my husband lost his job, we struggled to **pay the bills** for almost a year.
My weekend job at the hardware store isn't glamorous, but it **pays the bills**.

drill.sentence: With two kids in day care, my salary barely {{pays the bills}}.
drill.hint: is enough for our regular living costs (not *covers* …)

entries.related: *make ends meet* — just manage to pay for basic needs; *keep the lights on* — informal, earn enough to keep going; *a day job* — the job that pays while you follow another dream.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Without a job, usually for a period of time and not by choice.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and news: *be out of work*, *be put out of work*, *have been out of work for six months*. It sounds more everyday and a little softer than *unemployed*. Before a noun it is hyphenated: *an out-of-work actor*.
entries.pattern: be / be put out of work (for + period)
examples: When the factory closed, almost four hundred people were suddenly **out of work**.
My brother has been **out of work** since March, so he's living with my parents for now.
Weeks of storms kept the fishing boats in the harbor and put hundreds of crew members **out of work**.

drill.sentence: After the restaurant burned down, its whole staff was {{out of work}} for months while it was rebuilt.
drill.hint: without jobs (three words; not *unemployed*)

entries.related: *unemployed* — more formal and official; *between jobs* — a polite, positive way to say it; *laid off* — lost a job because the employer cut staff.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: An error that causes a lot of damage, expense or loss, in money or in other ways.
entries.usage: Common in news, sports, business and personal advice: *make a costly mistake*, *prove to be a costly mistake*, *avoid costly mistakes*. *Costly* can mean losing money, time, a game or a relationship, not only money. In casual speech people also say *an expensive mistake* when money is involved.
entries.pattern: make / avoid + a costly mistake; prove (to be) a costly mistake
examples: Skipping the home inspection was **a costly mistake**: the basement flooded the first spring.
The goalkeeper's **costly mistake** in the final minute handed the other team the championship.
Signing a lease without reading the fine print can be **a costly mistake**.

drill.sentence: Paying the contractor the full amount up front was {{a costly mistake}}; he disappeared after two days of work.
drill.hint: a blunder with a high price (adjective: not *expensive* or *big*; noun: not *error*)

entries.related: *an expensive mistake* — more casual, usually about money; *a fatal mistake* — one that ruins everything or causes death; *learn the hard way* — learn from a painful mistake.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Not expected at all; a total surprise.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and storytelling, after *be* or before a noun: *a completely unexpected call*. It is neutral and can describe good or bad surprises. *Totally unexpected* is more casual, and *came as a complete surprise* is a common alternative.
entries.pattern: be completely unexpected; a completely unexpected + call / result / gift
examples: Her resignation was **completely unexpected**; nobody at the office had any idea she was unhappy.
We got a **completely unexpected** call from a cousin we hadn't heard from in twenty years.
The small-town team's win in the state final was **completely unexpected**, even to their own fans.

drill.sentence: We'd only been dating for six months, so his proposal was {{completely unexpected}}.
drill.hint: not foreseen in any way (adverb + adjective; adverb not *totally* or *entirely*)

entries.related: *out of the blue* — informal, suddenly and without warning; *came as a shock* — unexpected and upsetting; *predictable* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To keep someone interested in something for a period of time.
entries.usage: Common when talking about teaching, speeches, books, movies and children, often with *can't*, *struggle to* or *for long*. *Get*, *grab* or *catch someone's attention* is about attracting it at the start; *hold* or *keep* it is about not losing it.
entries.pattern: hold someone's / the audience's attention (for + time)
examples: The speaker told funny stories from her own life, which **held the audience's attention** for a full hour.
Nothing **holds my four-year-old's attention** for more than five minutes, except dinosaurs.
The novel starts well, but the middle section didn't **hold my attention** at all.

drill.sentence: Our history teacher used old maps and short videos to {{hold our attention}} during the long afternoon classes.
drill.hint: stop us from getting bored (verb + *our* + noun; verb not *keep*, *grab* or *catch*)

entries.related: *grab someone's attention* — attract it suddenly; *keep someone's attention* — the same as *hold*; *lose someone's attention* — the opposite.

entries.label: noun + of + noun
entries.meaning: A feeling that your life or work has a clear aim and is worth doing.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, psychology and career advice, and in stories about retirement, volunteering or recovery: *give someone / find / lose a sense of purpose*. It is positive and a little serious. Adjectives often go before *sense*: *a strong / real / renewed sense of purpose*.
entries.pattern: give someone / find / lose + a sense of purpose
examples: After retiring, my father felt lost until volunteering at the food bank gave him **a sense of purpose** again.
Many young people say they want jobs with **a sense of purpose**, not just a good salary.
Losing his job took away his **sense of purpose** even more than his income.

drill.sentence: After the injury ended his football career, it took Jake years to find {{a sense of purpose}} again.
drill.hint: the feeling that his life had a clear aim (noun + *of* + noun; not *meaning* or *direction*)

entries.related: *a sense of direction* — knowing where your life is going; *a reason to get up in the morning* — informal, something that motivates you; *aimless* — the opposite, without a goal.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To stop being interested in something or someone that used to interest you.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation about hobbies, school, relationships and TV shows: *lose interest in* + noun or *-ing*. It also works without an object: *The kids quickly lost interest.* Usually there is no article before *interest*, but *lose all interest* is common for emphasis.
entries.pattern: lose (all) interest in + noun / -ing
examples: My son begged for a guitar for his birthday and then **lost interest in** it within a month.
A lot of viewers **lost interest in** the show after the main character was killed off.
If a date checks his phone all evening, I **lose interest** pretty fast.

drill.sentence: Ever since she started her new job, she seems to have {{lost interest in}} her old hobbies, even painting.
drill.hint: stopped caring about (verb + noun + preposition)

mistake.wrong: My daughter lost interest for the piano after a year.
mistake.right: My daughter lost interest in the piano after a year.
mistake.why: *Interest* takes *in*, as in *be interested in* and *show interest in*.

entries.related: *get bored with* — more casual; *go off something* — British, stop liking it; *take an interest in* — the opposite, start being interested.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Refusing to accept that something unpleasant is true, often because it is too painful to face.
entries.usage: It comes from psychology but is now very common in everyday talk, usually as *be in denial (about something)*. It is often a criticism or a gentle joke: *He's in denial about turning fifty.* *Still in denial* is a frequent combination.
entries.pattern: be (still) in denial (about + something)
examples: My dad's hearing is getting worse, but he's **in denial** and says everyone just mumbles.
For months after the breakup, she was **in denial**, telling friends they were just taking a break.
Some fans are still **in denial** about their star quarterback's retirement.

drill.sentence: He keeps saying his old car just needs a few small repairs, but he's {{in denial}}; it's falling apart.
drill.hint: refusing to face the truth (preposition + noun; not *kidding himself*)

entries.related: *bury your head in the sand* — ignore a problem and hope it goes away; *kid yourself* — informal, believe something false because you want to; *come to terms with* — finally accept it.

entries.label: noun phrase
entries.meaning: An activity that achieves nothing useful at all, so the time spent on it is lost.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and reviews, and clearly critical. *Total* and *utter* are common alternatives; *utter* sounds the most emphatic. It can be followed by *-ing*: *It's a complete waste of time arguing with him.*
entries.pattern: be a complete waste of time (-ing / to + verb)
examples: The training session was **a complete waste of time**; they just read the handbook out loud for two hours.
Honestly, that cooking show is **a complete waste of time**: nobody on it actually cooks anything.
Trying to change my uncle's mind about money is **a complete waste of time**.

drill.sentence: I drove across town to return the jacket, but the store had closed early. What {{a complete waste of time}}.
drill.hint: a trip that achieved nothing (adjective: not *total* or *utter*)

entries.related: *a waste of breath* — talking that will not change anything; *pointless* — without a purpose; *time well spent* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To ask another expert, especially another doctor, to check a diagnosis, judgment or price before you decide.
entries.usage: Most common about medical decisions, but also used for car repairs, legal advice and home repairs. *Get* is the normal verb; *seek a second opinion* is more formal. It is a polite way to say you are not sure the first expert is right.
entries.pattern: get a second opinion (from + expert) (on / about + something)
examples: The first surgeon wanted to operate right away, so my mother **got a second opinion** before agreeing.
The mechanic quoted me two thousand dollars for the brakes, so I'm going to **get a second opinion**.
Before you sign the contract, it might be worth **getting a second opinion** from a lawyer.

drill.sentence: The vet said our dog needed expensive hip surgery, so we took him to another clinic to {{get a second opinion}}.
drill.hint: have another expert check the diagnosis (adjective: not *another*)

entries.related: *double-check* — check again yourself; *seek a second opinion* — the same, more formal; *take someone's word for it* — trust the first expert without checking.

entries.label: adverb + adjective
entries.meaning: Making you feel tired, empty and worn out inside because of the strong feelings involved.
entries.usage: Common in conversation about caregiving, conflict, breakups, hospital stays and demanding jobs. It describes what causes the feeling (*The visit was emotionally draining*); the person who feels it is *emotionally drained*. *Exhausting* alone is broader and can also mean physically tiring.
entries.pattern: be emotionally draining (for + someone); an emotionally draining + day / week / experience
examples: Taking care of my grandmother after her stroke was rewarding, but **emotionally draining**.
Working in the emergency room is **emotionally draining**, so many nurses leave within a few years.
After an **emotionally draining** week of court hearings, the family finally got some good news.

drill.sentence: Helping my parents sell the house I grew up in was {{emotionally draining}}; every room brought back memories.
drill.hint: tiring for the heart, not the body (adverb + adjective; adjective not *exhausting*)

entries.related: *emotionally drained* — how the person feels; *heartbreaking* — very sad; *a rollercoaster* — informal, an experience full of ups and downs.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A member of your immediate family, such as a parent, child, brother or sister, and sometimes a grandparent.
entries.usage: Common in official contexts (forms, hospital rules, company leave policies) and in conversation. The opposite is *a distant relative*, such as a second cousin. *Immediate family* means the same group and is common in rules and invitations.
entries.pattern: a close relative (of + someone); the death / illness of a close relative
examples: Many companies give three days of paid leave after the death of **a close relative**.
Only **close relatives** were allowed to visit him in intensive care.
We kept the wedding small: just **close relatives** and a few old friends.

drill.sentence: I didn't want to share details at work, so I just told my boss that {{a close relative}} was in the hospital.
drill.hint: parent, child or sibling (adjective + noun; not *family member*)

entries.related: *a distant relative* — the opposite; *next of kin* — the closest living relative, a legal and medical term; *extended family* — aunts, uncles, cousins and so on.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To write down or save information regularly so that it can be checked later.
entries.usage: Common in practical advice from doctors, accountants and lawyers: *keep a record of your expenses / symptoms / hours*. *Keep track of* stresses following something as it changes; *keep a record* stresses having written proof. The plural *keep records* is usual for official documents: *The clinic keeps records for seven years.*
entries.pattern: keep a record of + expenses / symptoms / hours / calls
examples: My doctor asked me to **keep a record of** everything I eat for two weeks.
If your landlord won't fix the heat, **keep a record of** every call and email.
Freelancers should **keep a record of** their expenses, since many of them are tax-deductible.

drill.sentence: I {{keep a record of}} every run in a notebook: the distance, the time and how my knee felt.
drill.hint: regularly write down, as proof (verb + noun + *of*; not *track* or *log*)

entries.related: *keep track of* — follow something as it changes; *log* — record events in order, often in a system; *document* — formal, record in detail as evidence.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To come into someone's thoughts, often briefly or for the first time.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation, especially in the negative: *It never crossed my mind (that …)* means you did not even consider it. The subject is the idea, or *it* + a *that*-clause or *to* + verb; the person appears as a possessive (*crossed her mind*). *The thought crossed my mind* is a common way to admit you briefly considered something.
entries.pattern: it (never) crossed someone's mind (that … / to + verb); the thought crossed my mind
examples: It never **crossed my mind** that she might be allergic to nuts, so I didn't ask.
Did it ever **cross your mind** to call and tell us you'd be late?
The thought of moving back home **crossed my mind** more than once during that first winter in Chicago.

drill.sentence: I was so focused on packing that it never {{crossed my mind}} to check whether my passport had expired.
drill.hint: came into my thoughts (verb + *my* + noun; not *occurred to me*)

entries.related: *occur to someone* — the same, slightly more neutral; *spring to mind* — come to mind quickly and easily; *slip someone's mind* — be forgotten.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Money that you receive regularly and reliably, for example from a salary or rent.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and personal finance: *have / need / provide a steady income*. *Steady* stresses that the money keeps coming without gaps, not that it is large. *A stable income* is very close, and *a regular paycheck* is a more casual American way to say it.
entries.pattern: have / need / provide + a steady income (from + source)
examples: Freelancing was exciting, but after two years I wanted **a steady income** and health insurance.
The apartment above their garage gives my parents **a steady income** in retirement.
Banks prefer to lend to people with **a steady income**, even if it's not very high.

drill.sentence: My dad was a mail carrier for thirty years; he always said {{a steady income}} mattered more than an exciting job.
drill.hint: money that comes in reliably (adjective: not *stable*, *regular* or *reliable*)

entries.related: *a stable income* — very close; *a regular paycheck* — American, casual; *live paycheck to paycheck* — have just enough money until the next payment.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Too far away to touch or get, or too expensive or difficult to achieve.
entries.usage: Used literally, as in the safety warning *Keep out of reach of children*, and very often about prices and goals: *Tickets were out of reach for most fans.* With prices and goals, the person usually follows *for*. *Within reach* is the opposite.
entries.pattern: be / keep something out of reach (of / for + someone)
examples: We moved the cookie jar to the top shelf, safely **out of reach** of the kids.
With prices this high, a house in the city is **out of reach** for most young couples.
After two losses, a spot in the playoffs now seems **out of reach**.

drill.sentence: The keys fell behind the radiator, just {{out of reach}}, so I had to use a coat hanger to get them out.
drill.hint: too far to grab (three words; not *beyond …*)

entries.related: *within reach* — the opposite, close enough to get or achieve; *unaffordable* — too expensive; *a long shot* — something unlikely to succeed.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To gain new experiences and widen your knowledge and understanding of the world.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, education and travel writing, and in advice to young people. The possessive changes with the person (*broaden her / their horizons*), and the subject can also be the experience: *Travel broadens your horizons.* *Expand your horizons* means the same and is also common in American English.
entries.pattern: broaden your / someone's horizons (by + -ing); something broadens your horizons
examples: Spending a year in Japan really **broadened my horizons**; I came back seeing my own country differently.
My grandmother took a pottery class at seventy-five, just to **broaden her horizons**.
The program sends rural high school students to summer camps in big cities to **broaden their horizons**.

drill.sentence: Working on a cruise ship for two years {{broadened his horizons}}: he made friends from over forty countries.
drill.hint: gave him a wider view of the world (verb: not *expanded* or *widened*; not *opened his eyes*)

entries.related: *expand your horizons* — the same; *open someone's eyes* — make them realize something new; *narrow-minded* — the opposite, not open to new ideas.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Strictly, the money you have left after taxes; in everyday use, the money left to spend or save after rent, bills and other necessities.
entries.usage: Common in economics, news and conversation about money: *have more / less / little disposable income*. Economists use *discretionary income* for money left after necessities, but in conversation most people say *disposable income* for both. It is usually uncountable: *not much disposable income*.
entries.pattern: have (more / little) disposable income; a rise / fall in disposable income
examples: Once the student loans were paid off, we finally had some **disposable income** for travel.
With rent taking half her paycheck, she has very little **disposable income**.
When **disposable income** falls, restaurants and movie theaters are usually the first to feel it.

drill.sentence: After rent, groceries and the car payment, I have about three hundred dollars of {{disposable income}} a month.
drill.hint: money left to spend freely (adjective + noun; not *spending money* or *discretionary*)

entries.related: *spending money* — casual, money for fun and small purchases; *discretionary income* — technical, left after taxes and necessities; *gross income* — before taxes.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To act quickly and with energy to use a good chance when it comes.
entries.usage: Common in speeches, news, business and motivational writing; in conversation people more often say *jump at the chance* or *take the opportunity*. It is often followed by *to* + verb. *Seize* suggests speed and determination, while *take* is neutral, so using *seize* for small things sounds playful.
entries.pattern: seize the opportunity (to + verb)
examples: When her manager left suddenly, she **seized the opportunity** and asked to lead the team.
The kids were finally asleep, so we **seized the opportunity** to watch a movie without interruptions.
Local farmers **seized the opportunity** when a big grocery chain started buying from nearby farms.

drill.sentence: When the shoe store next door went out of business, the café owner {{seized the opportunity}} to expand into the space.
drill.hint: quickly and eagerly used that chance (verb: not *took*; noun: not *chance*)

entries.related: *take the opportunity* — neutral, less urgent; *jump at the chance* — informal, accept eagerly; *miss the boat* — lose a chance by acting too slowly.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To notice something and pay attention to it, so that you remember it or act on it later.
entries.usage: A little formal; common in instructions, announcements, news and work emails: *Please take note of the new deadline.* There is no article before *note*. Do not confuse it with *make a note of*, which means writing something down; in casual speech people usually say *notice* or *pay attention to*.
entries.pattern: take note of + something; please take note (that …)
examples: Investors **took note of** the company's falling sales and started selling their shares.
Please **take note of** the emergency exits nearest you before takeoff.
The coach **took note of** which players stayed late to practice.

drill.sentence: Before giving back our deposit, the landlord walked through the apartment and {{took note of}} every scratch on the floor.
drill.hint: noticed and kept in mind (verb + noun + *of*; noun not *notice*)

entries.related: *make a note of* — write down; *take notice of* — pay attention to, often in the negative: *nobody took any notice*; *sit up and take notice* — suddenly start paying attention.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Pay that is high enough for a worker to cover basic needs such as housing, food and health care.
entries.usage: Common in news and in discussions about pay and jobs. It is different from the legal *minimum wage*, which in many places is lower. Typical patterns are *pay (someone) a living wage* and *earn a living wage*; some cities and companies calculate their own figure for it.
entries.pattern: pay / earn + a living wage
examples: Two part-time jobs still didn't add up to **a living wage**, so he moved in with roommates.
The coffee chain says it pays all its baristas **a living wage**, plus health insurance.
Many young musicians find it hard to earn **a living wage** from streaming alone.

drill.sentence: The family-owned grocery store raised its hourly pay to twenty-two dollars because the owner believes every worker should earn {{a living wage}}.
drill.hint: pay that covers basic needs (adjective: not *decent* or *fair*)

entries.related: *minimum wage* — the lowest pay allowed by law; *make a living* — earn enough money to live on; *scrape by* — just barely manage with little money.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Not suitable for a situation, or not comfortable and not fitting in with the people around you.
entries.usage: Used about people (*feel / look out of place*) and about things that do not match their setting: *That modern lamp looks out of place in the farmhouse.* *Feel out of place* is the most common pattern and describes social discomfort. Before a noun it is hyphenated (*an out-of-place remark*), but that use is less common.
entries.pattern: feel / look / seem + out of place (in + setting / among + people)
examples: I showed up in jeans, and everyone else was in suits, so I felt completely **out of place**.
A shiny glass tower would look **out of place** in this old fishing village.
His joke about money seemed **out of place** at the funeral.

drill.sentence: As the only person over forty at the concert, my mom felt a little {{out of place}}, but she danced anyway.
drill.hint: as if she didn't belong (three words; not *awkward*)

entries.related: *like a fish out of water* — informal, very uncomfortable in an unfamiliar setting; *fit in* — the opposite, feel accepted; *inappropriate* — not suitable, a stronger criticism.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To decide what you think about someone or something after getting some information or experience.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, news and advice, with *about* or *of*: *form an opinion of someone*. It suggests a process of judging, so it often comes with *before*, *until*, *too quickly* or *your own*: *form your own opinion*. *Form an impression* is lighter and faster, based on a first look.
entries.pattern: form an opinion (of / about + someone / something); form your own opinion
examples: After two weeks at her new school, my daughter had already **formed an opinion** of every teacher.
Read the whole article before you **form an opinion**; the headline is misleading.
Jurors are told not to **form an opinion** until they've heard all the evidence.

drill.sentence: I haven't seen the movie yet, so I can't really {{form an opinion}} about the ending.
drill.hint: decide what I think (verb + noun; verb not *have* or *give*)

entries.related: *form an impression* — a quick first judgment; *make up your mind* — decide between options; *have an open mind* — be ready to consider new ideas.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: A large amount of money that a person or company must pay as a punishment for breaking a rule or law.
entries.usage: Very common in news and conversation; *hefty* also goes with *bill*, *fee* and *price tag*. Typical verbs are *face*, *get*, *pay* and *be hit with*. It stresses that the amount really hurts, often with a touch of sympathy or humor.
entries.pattern: face / get / pay / be hit with + a hefty fine (for + -ing)
examples: He got **a hefty fine** for parking in a fire lane outside the mall.
The construction company was hit with **a hefty fine** for blocking the sidewalk for six months without a permit.
Fishing without a license in this state can mean **a hefty fine**.

drill.sentence: The landlord had to pay {{a hefty fine}} after inspectors found no working smoke detectors in the building.
drill.hint: a painfully large penalty (adjective: not *big*, *large*, *heavy* or *steep*)

entries.related: *a slap on the wrist* — a punishment that is too light; *a parking ticket* — a fine for illegal parking; *a hefty price tag* — a high price.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To help someone remember something by reminding them of the facts or details.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, meetings, classrooms and courtrooms. *Let me refresh your memory* can sound slightly sarcastic, suggesting the listener has conveniently forgotten. *Refresh my memory* is a polite way to ask for a reminder: *Can you refresh my memory on her name?*
entries.pattern: refresh someone's memory (about / on + topic); let me refresh your memory
examples: Before the exam, I reread the first three chapters to **refresh my memory**.
You don't remember promising to help me move? Let me **refresh your memory**.
The lawyer showed the witness a photo to **refresh her memory** about the night of the accident.

drill.sentence: I'd forgotten most of the plot, so I watched the first season again to {{refresh my memory}} before the new one came out.
drill.hint: help myself recall the details (verb: not *jog*)

entries.related: *jog someone's memory* — trigger a memory with a small clue; *remind someone* — plainer; *ring a bell* — seem familiar.

entries.label: prepositional phrase
entries.meaning: Owing money to a person, bank or company.
entries.usage: Very common in conversation and personal finance, with *be*, *go into*, *get out of* and *deep in*. The amount goes before it (*ten thousand dollars in debt*), and the lender follows *to*. *I'm in your debt* is a formal way to say you owe someone a favor.
entries.pattern: be (deep) in debt (to + lender); go into / get out of debt
examples: Many students finish college forty thousand dollars **in debt**.
My parents hated being **in debt**, so they paid cash for everything, even cars.
The owners were so deeply **in debt** that they had to sell the restaurant.

drill.sentence: He borrowed from friends to keep the business going, and by the end of the year he was {{in debt}} to almost everyone he knew.
drill.hint: owing money (preposition + noun; not *indebted*)

entries.related: *broke* — informal, having no money; *in the red* — losing money, about a business or account; *debt-free* — the opposite.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To say something nice to someone, praising them or something about them.
entries.usage: *Pay* is the classic verb; in casual speech people also say *give someone a compliment* or simply *compliment someone on something*. The person usually comes right after the verb: *She paid me a compliment.* *A backhanded compliment* is praise that hides an insult.
entries.pattern: pay someone a compliment (on + something)
examples: A stranger on the subway **paid me a compliment** on my coat, and it made my whole morning.
My boss rarely **pays anyone a compliment**, so when she said I'd done great work, I was thrilled.
When someone **pays you a compliment**, just say thank you instead of arguing with it.

drill.sentence: At the reunion, my old math teacher {{paid me a compliment}} that I still remember: she said I'd always asked the best questions.
drill.hint: said something nice about me (verb: not *gave*)

mistake.wrong: He made me a nice compliment on my dress.
mistake.right: He paid me a nice compliment on my dress.
mistake.why: English uses *pay* or *give* a compliment; *make a compliment* is a translation from languages such as French, German or Spanish.

entries.related: *flatter* — praise too much, often to get something; *a backhanded compliment* — praise with a hidden insult; *fish for compliments* — try to get people to praise you.

entries.label: noun + noun
entries.meaning: A win in an election, or in another vote, by a very large margin.
entries.usage: Common in news about elections at every level, from national races to school boards; *win by a landslide* and *win in a landslide* are both common. It is also used humorously for any small vote among friends or coworkers. The literal *landslide* is a mass of earth sliding down a hill.
entries.pattern: win a landslide victory; win by / in a landslide
examples: After **a landslide victory** in November, the new mayor promised to fix the city's potholes first.
My daughter's campaign for class president ended in **a landslide victory**: she got every vote but two.
The plan to build a new library won **a landslide victory** at the polls, with three out of four voters in favor.

drill.sentence: When our book club voted on the next novel, the mystery won {{a landslide victory}}: eleven votes to one.
drill.hint: a win by a huge margin (noun + noun; not *overwhelming* or *crushing*)

entries.related: *win hands down* — win easily; *a narrow victory* — the opposite, a win by a small margin; *a sweep* — winning every race or award.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To phone someone who tried to call you, usually after you missed their call or got their message.
entries.usage: Neutral and very common at work and in everyday life: *Thanks for returning my call.* *Call someone back* is the more casual equivalent. Not returning calls is a common complaint about landlords, contractors and offices, often in the plural: *He never returns my calls.*
entries.pattern: return someone's call(s); thanks for returning my call
examples: I left three messages with the insurance company, but nobody has **returned my call**.
Sorry I didn't **return your call** yesterday; my phone died at the beach.
A good contractor **returns your calls**, even when the news is bad.

drill.sentence: The doctor's office promised to {{return my call}} by noon, but I'm still waiting to hear from them.
drill.hint: reply to my phone message (verb + *my* + noun; not the casual form with *back*)

entries.related: *call someone back* — the same, more casual; *get back to someone* — reply later, by phone or email; *screen your calls* — check who is calling before you answer.

entries.label: adjective + noun
entries.meaning: Someone you do not know at all and have never met before.
entries.usage: Common in conversation and stories, often to stress surprise at someone's kindness, rudeness or trust. *A total stranger* and *a perfect stranger* mean the same; *perfect* sounds a little old-fashioned. *Be no stranger to something* is different: it means having a lot of experience of it.
entries.pattern: a complete stranger; tell / trust / help + a complete stranger
examples: My car broke down on the highway, and **a complete stranger** stopped and changed my tire.
I'd never give my bank details to **a complete stranger** on the phone.
It's strange how you can tell **a complete stranger** on a plane things you'd never tell your family.

drill.sentence: My grandmother talks to everyone; she'll tell {{a complete stranger}} at the bus stop all about her grandkids.
drill.hint: someone she has never met (adjective: not *total* or *perfect*)

entries.related: *an acquaintance* — someone you know a little; *a familiar face* — someone you recognize; *be no stranger to* — have experience of.

entries.label: verb + noun
entries.meaning: To suggest something indirectly, instead of saying it clearly, hoping the other person will understand.
entries.usage: Common in conversation, especially about gifts, romance and work: *drop a hint (about something)*, *drop hints that …*. *Drop a big hint* or *a not-so-subtle hint* means it is quite obvious. If the other person understands, they *take the hint* or *get the hint*.
entries.pattern: drop a hint (about + something / that …); drop hints
examples: She **dropped a hint** about wanting a new watch by leaving the catalog open on the kitchen table.
My boss **dropped a few hints** that layoffs were coming, so I started updating my résumé.
I kept **dropping hints** that I was tired, but our guests stayed until midnight.

drill.sentence: My roommate never washes his dishes, so I {{dropped a hint}} by leaving a brand-new sponge on his plate.
drill.hint: suggested it indirectly (verb + noun; verb not *gave*)

entries.related: *take the hint* — understand what was suggested; *beat around the bush* — avoid saying something directly; *spell it out* — say it clearly, the opposite.

entries.label: adverb + participle
entries.meaning: With no free rooms, seats, tables or appointments left.
entries.usage: Common for hotels, restaurants, flights, classes and appointments with doctors or hairdressers: *We're fully booked tonight.* It is neutral and polite, typical in customer service. *Booked solid* and *booked up* are more casual; for tickets to a show or game, people say *sold out*.
entries.pattern: be fully booked (for + date / until + time)
examples: Every hotel near the stadium was **fully booked**, so we stayed an hour away.
I'm sorry, Dr. Patel is **fully booked** this week, but I can put you on the waiting list.
The cooking class was **fully booked** within an hour of opening registration.

drill.sentence: We tried to get a table at the new Thai place for Saturday night, but it was {{fully booked}} until the end of the month.
drill.hint: had no free tables at all (adverb + participle; not the casual forms with *solid* or *up*)

entries.related: *booked solid* — informal, completely full; *sold out* — no tickets left; *available* — the opposite, free to book.
